Notation and method
N
Observations in the shared synthetic sample.
ε (epsilon)
Privacy budget per run. Smaller values add more noise.
r
Pearson correlation from −1 to +1. Positive means higher values tend to go together. Negative means higher values of one tend to go with lower values of the other. Partial r measures that pattern after accounting for the control.
Δr
Private median partial r minus original partial r.
*
Less than 5% of either variable’s variance remains after adjustment in the original sample.

The vertical mark shows the original estimate. The dot shows the middle estimate when runs are sorted, and the band covers about 8 in 10 estimates. Each run uses the same data and a fresh draw of Laplace noise. The stabilization floor limits how close the noisy covariance can get to singular. Raising it can make estimates more stable and pull them toward zero.

How the simulation works

From painting to synthetic data

The lab normalizes the painted weights and draws one input histogram of N observations. Each run privatizes that same histogram and then draws N synthetic observations. Reuse a seed to compare methods with the same input draw.

How each method adds noise

  • Laplace per cell. Add independent Laplace noise with scale 2/ε to each count, clamp negatives, and normalize. If every count is zero, use a uniform distribution.
  • Projected Laplace. Start with the same noisy counts and find the nearest nonnegative table summing to the public N. The shared offset often removes small noise-only counts.
  • Private moments. Map ordered buckets to [−1, 1]. Spend ε/5 on each of the means of X, Y, X², Y², and XY, using the range divided by N for sensitivity. Fit a regularized maximum-entropy distribution to target Pearson correlation.
  • Multiscale quadtree. Split ε across the levels of a public spatial tree. Noise the region counts at each level, combine estimates across scales, and reconcile children to their parent totals. Hierarchical consistency ↗
  • Marginals + coarse blocks. Spend ε/3 on each of the two fine axis histograms and a coarse joint table. Reconcile the block totals to the noisy axis histograms, then distribute mass inside each block using the two within-block marginals. Inference from noisy measurements ↗
  • Low-frequency cosine. Split ε across the nonconstant 2D cosine modes up to the selected total order. Higher cutoffs retain finer detail and increase the noise scale per coefficient. Noise the bounded coefficient sums, invert the truncated transform, and project to a nonnegative table with total N. A cutoff of zero gives a uniform fit. Private orthogonal series ↗

What the comparisons measure

Loss is synthetic minus painted probability, so it includes both sampling variation and privacy noise. Joint TV is half the sum of absolute cell losses. Axis TV averages the same distance on the X and Y marginals. Pearson r uses bucket indices and is undefined if either axis has zero variance.

Partial correlations use separate synthetic data from the Input tab. They measure how two variables move together after removing the linear relationship each has with the chosen control.

All methods use fixed-size, replace-one adjacency and a per-run ε. The seeded simulation, original table, and loss tables are for exploration with synthetic inputs. Publishing multiple private runs on real data would require composition accounting.
